summary: Before a client can use TLS Encrypted ClientHello (ECH), it must learn the server's ECH configuration. This specification describes how to publish that configuration in DNS using SVCB or HTTPS resource records, so clients can fetch it before connecting.

eli5.summary: Before sending a secret note, you need the right lock. This lets a server leave its lock details in a public phone book, so visitors can look them up first.

questions: how to publish ech config in dns
why can ech not fall back to plain tls
subtitle: How a server publishes its Encrypted ClientHello settings in DNS so clients can find them before connecting.

tldr.problem: A client must know a server's ECH configuration before its first connection attempt, or it cannot encrypt its ClientHello.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an ech SvcParam for SVCB and HTTPS DNS records that carries the ECHConfigList, and sets rules for servers and clients, including no fallback to a non-ECH connection.
tldr.outcome: DNS becomes the primary bootstrap mechanism for ECH. The security caveats are mixed record sets, which allow downgrade attacks, and DNS lookups that still reveal the server name.

today: RFC 9848 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2026 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It works together with the ECH specification in RFC 9849 and the SVCB framework in RFC 9460.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Service Bindings framework (RFC 9460) lets server operators publish a description of their service in the DNS using SVCB or HTTPS records. Each record describes one alternative endpoint and holds a set of SvcParams that clients can use to improve the privacy, security and performance of their connection.

RFC 9848 defines one new SvcParam for TLS Encrypted ClientHello (ECH, RFC 9849). It can be used in SVCB, HTTPS or any future SVCB-compatible record, and is intended to be the primary bootstrap mechanism for ECH.
sections.eli5: A server can leave a note in the public phone book about how to talk to it. This document adds a new line to that note: the details needed to hide who you are visiting.

sections.title: The ech SvcParam
sections.content:
The ech SvcParamKey carries the ECH configuration of an alternative endpoint. It applies to all schemes that use TLS-based protocols, including DTLS (RFC 9147) and QUIC version 1 (RFC 9001), unless otherwise specified.

On the wire, the value is an ECHConfigList from the ECH specification, including its redundant length prefix. In presentation format, it is that list in Base 64 (RFC 4648), chosen to simplify integration with TLS server software. To keep parsing simple, the value MUST NOT contain escape sequences.
sections.eli5: The new line in the note is a long string of letters and numbers. It is a packed-up set of instructions that the visitor's computer knows how to unpack.

sections.title: Server Requirements
sections.content:
A publisher of a record with an ech parameter MUST ensure that every IP address of the TargetName belongs to a server that has the matching private key or is authoritative for the public name. Otherwise, connections will fail entirely.

Those servers SHOULD support a protocol version compatible with ECH. At the time of writing these are TLS 1.3, DTLS 1.3 and QUIC version 1. Without one, each connection attempt has to be retried, which delays the connection and wastes resources.
sections.eli5: If the note says to use a certain secret lock, every door the note points to must have the matching key. Otherwise visitors get stuck outside.

sections.title: Client Behavior
sections.content:
No fallback. Normally an SVCB-optional client may fall back to a direct connection if all SVCB options fail. For ECH this is unsuitable, since fallback would negate its privacy benefit. So an ECH-capable, SVCB-optional client MUST switch to SVCB-reliant connection establishment if SVCB resolution succeeded and all alternative endpoints have an ech SvcParam.

Two ClientHellos. With ECH, the ClientHello is split into an unencrypted outer one and an encrypted inner one. The outer one is controlled by the ECHConfig. The inner one is used to reach the service, so other SVCB parameters can shape it. For example, the ALPN rules from the SVCB specification apply only to the inner ClientHello, and its Server Name Indication names the desired service.

Ordering. Because the ech parameter changes the ClientHello, ECH-capable clients MUST NOT send any TLS ClientHello until SVCB resolution has completed. As a latency optimization, clients MAY prefetch DNS records that are only used when ech is absent.
sections.eli5: Once the phone book says to use the secret lock, the visitor must not try the unlocked side door instead. And they must look in the phone book before knocking at all.

sections.title: Interaction with HTTP Alt-Svc
sections.content:
HTTP clients that support both Alt-Svc (RFC 7838) and HTTPS records can use them together if they only make connection attempts consistent with both. No ECH parameter is defined for Alt-Svc, so an attempt that uses ECH counts as consistent with an Alt-Svc value that does not mention ECH.

An origin that publishes ech in its HTTPS record SHOULD also publish an HTTPS record with ech for every alt-authority in its Alt-Svc values. Otherwise clients might reveal the server name in an unencrypted ClientHello to an alt-authority. If all HTTPS records for an alt-authority carry ech, the client MUST use SVCB-reliant behavior for that record set.
sections.eli5: If the server also lists backup addresses, each backup needs its own lock details too, or a visitor could end up shouting the secret name at an unprepared door.

sections.title: Deployment Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives zone-file examples for common setups.

  • A simple zone with the same HTTPS 1 . ech=... record on the apex and on www, which works for clients with or without HTTPS record support.
  • A service with two server pools that have different ECH configurations, published as two SVCB records.
  • An aliasing-based CDN, where the customer zone points to the CDN's pool name and the CDN publishes the ech value.
  • A domain reachable only with ECH, using mandatory=ech.
  • A multi-CDN customer that switches between two CDN pools on the server side.
  • A DNS server that supports ECH, combining ech with alpn and dohpath.
sections.eli5: The document shows sample phone-book entries for different kinds of websites, from a tiny one with one server to a big one that uses several delivery companies.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mixed record sets. A set containing some records with ech and some without is open to a downgrade attack: a network intermediary can block the ECH endpoints and push the client to a non-ECH endpoint. This is NOT RECOMMENDED, though it may be unavoidable when combining providers or rolling out in stages. Zone owners who do it SHOULD give the ech records a lower SvcPriority value, meaning more preferred.

Limits of ECH. The protection is limited to an anonymity set: all ECH-enabled domains behind a client-facing server that share a configuration. An attacker who can enumerate the set can guess the encrypted name with probability at least 1/K for K domains, and traffic analysis may do better.

DNS still sees the name. This specification does not hide the server name from the DNS resolver. Without authenticated encryption between client and resolver, an on-path attacker can also learn it.

Blocked lookups. An attacker who prevents SVCB resolution can deny the client the benefits, even with DNSSEC and a secure transport, and the client may then send its ClientHello in cleartext. The SVCB specification recommends abandoning the connection attempt when such an attack is detected.
sections.eli5: Hiding the name in the secret note does not hide it from the phone book keeper, and someone could tear out the page so visitors never see the secret lock details.
